title: Zomato Checks Gurgaon Restaurant Menus for Undeclared 'Analogue' Paneer
excerpt: The food-delivery platform has started menu-level audits of eateries in Gurgaon to verify that dishes sold as paneer are not made with cheaper dairy substitutes, according to the Indian Express. The move is the first on-the-ground enforcement of Zomato's zero-tolerance policy on analogue dairy announced last month.
body:
• Zomato has begun menu-level checks at Gurgaon restaurants to verify dishes sold as paneer contain no undeclared analogue dairy, according to the Indian Express.
  • The audits enforce Zomato's August 31 zero-tolerance policy, under which declared 'analogue dairy' dishes were delisted and non-compliant restaurants were warned of removal.
  • Analogue paneer mimics dairy paneer using vegetable oils, starches and emulsifiers; passing it off as real paneer violates the Food Safety and Standards Act.
  • The checks come as Maharashtra and Telangana ban artificial paneer for a year and Haryana seizes 7,500 kg of suspected fake paneer headed for Delhi.

Zomato has started checking the menus of restaurants in Gurgaon for dishes that claim to be made with paneer but use cheaper "analogue" substitutes, according to the Indian Express. The audits are the platform's first on-the-ground enforcement of the zero-tolerance policy against analogue dairy it announced on August 31.

The question is simple: does a restaurant's paneer tikka or shahi paneer contain dairy paneer, or a lookalike built from plant oils and starches? A menu that says paneer while the kitchen serves an imitation risks delisting under Zomato's policy.

Context & background

Analogue paneer mimics traditional paneer in look and texture, but some or all of its milk components are replaced with vegetable oils or fats, starches, plant proteins, emulsifiers and stabilisers. As Mint explained, calling it "fake paneer" can mislead — an analogue product is not automatically adulterated. What matters is whether consumers are told what they are eating.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) said as much on April 29, when its public notice on cheese analogues stated that a cheese analogue cannot be sold as paneer. It directed manufacturers to use accurate product names when supplying eateries, and asked restaurants to train procurement teams and chefs, monitor incoming raw materials, disclose analogue use on menus or display boards, and test raw materials regularly.

State governments have gone further. Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration banned the manufacture, sale and storage of artificial analogue paneer for a year; Telangana imposed its own one-year ban this past week after enforcement raids. This week Haryana authorities seized 7,500 kg of suspected fake paneer headed for Delhi markets.

Against that backdrop, Zomato announced on August 31 that it would no longer tolerate analogue dishes on its platform. Dishes declared to contain "analogue dairy" were switched off with immediate effect, restaurants unable to switch to natural dairy were told to drop the items from their menus, and partners were ordered to review supplier labels and ingredient declarations so listings match what is actually served.

"At Zomato, our core mission is better food for more people, and that means safeguarding customer health and upholding clear standards for what's listed and served by our restaurant partners. This policy reflects that commitment, one we're taking together with partners who share it."

— Aditya Mangla, CEO, Zomato

Impact & analysis

Gurgaon is a natural place to start. The city packs a dense concentration of restaurants, cloud kitchens and corporate office clusters — exactly the kind of high-volume delivery market where menu accuracy is hardest to police. A policy announced from headquarters means little unless someone verifies what reaches the customer.

The economics explain the temptation. Analogue paneer costs far less to produce than dairy paneer. A restaurant that serves an imitation while charging dairy prices pockets the difference — and a customer who cannot inspect the dish before it arrives has no way to tell.

Zomato's leverage is blunt. "If a restaurant is found to be non-compliant, Zomato reserves the right to delist such restaurants from the platform, in addition to taking any other action available to us under our policies and applicable law," the company said. It also reserved the right to recover any loss, cost or damage it incurs when non-compliant products reach customers.

"If a restaurant is found to be non-compliant, Zomato reserves the right to delist such restaurants from the platform, in addition to taking any other action available to us under our policies and applicable law."

— Zomato, statement to restaurant partners

Diaspora angle

For the Indian diaspora, paneer is not just another menu item — it is a staple protein for millions of vegetarian families, and a dish NRI parents order for children visiting or studying in India. A family in Edison or Brampton ordering dinner for relatives in Gurgaon wants the paneer on the table to be paneer. Platform-level rules travel faster than state-by-state regulation, and Zomato's checks reach the exact kitchens diaspora families use when they are back home.

What's next

The key question is whether the Gurgaon checks are a pilot or a one-off. Zomato has not said whether menu audits will extend to Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and other major delivery markets — or whether it will publish what the checks find. Transparency about enforcement outcomes would do more for consumer trust than the policy announcement itself.

Watch also for the industry response. Swiggy, Zomato's main rival, has not announced a comparable analogue-dairy policy; competitive pressure may force its hand. And with several states imposing year-long bans, the FSSAI may face calls to standardise the rules nationally rather than leaving enforcement to a patchwork of state orders and platform policies.
image_caption: A malai paneer pizza topped with peppers and onions. Zomato has flagged Gurgaon restaurant menus using undeclared analogue paneer and synthetic dairy in place of real paneer.
nri_angle: Paneer is a staple protein for vegetarian diaspora families, who order delivery for relatives in India when visiting; Zomato's menu checks give NRI customers confidence the paneer served is genuine dairy, not a cheap substitute.
author: Diaspora Desk
